The Mortlake house has offered Septimus Gedge three times the charter's worth at the quarter-day sale.
The Widows' Row charter has hung in Septimus Gedge's window for thirty years as his shop's sample of an old hand; it was the first proof his father ever bought.
At first light six days ago Jacky Furlong, the eighth ring's lamp-boy, fell from the Pashley bridge into the court below when its rail gave way, and died.
The Pashley house blames Colin Ebbs, the mason's apprentice who mended the bridge's rail last month, and means to have him flogged at the court's post.
Dame Ermengarde Pashley has told her household she will sell the Pashley house's lower rooms.

Lucius Dray, steward to the Pashley house, loosened the bridge's rail in the night, meaning Dame Ermengarde Pashley to fall when she crossed at first light, as she always does: she was going to sell the lower rooms his family has lived in for three generations. Jacky Furlong crossed first that morning, to light the bridge lamps.
Colin Ebbs spent the night before Jacky Furlong's fall at the stone-tenders' lodge, at the vigil for a dead master, with twenty others.
The rail was loosened for whoever crossed the Pashley bridge first; every morning but that one, Dame Ermengarde Pashley crossed it first.
Hamnet Kemble, keeper of the Kemble bathhouse in the Ninth Ring's fourth ring, died this spring.

Denzil Kemble claims the bathhouse as his father promised it to him as a boy, and means to let it to a Seated house as a private bath; Joyce Kemble claims it for the ten years she ran it, and means to bring her brother in to stoke.

Both are partly right. Hamnet Kemble promised the bathhouse to his son when the boy was small, before an archive clerk; on his last night he told Joyce it was hers for as long as she kept it. Neither promise was entered in the house's line.
Whoever wins the bathhouse, Abram Stoke loses the furnace room he has slept in for thirty years.

Forty years ago Simon Pargeter, a copyist the archive sent to list what was left at half-ruined Firststone, cut a leaf from the First-Stone House's old house-book and sold it in the Ninth Ring; Hereward Ambler bought it in good faith as a curiosity, and it has stayed in the Ambler house since he died.

Ruʻo of the First-Stone House has told the pilgrims at the Founding Stone that the First-Stone leaf will lie at the Stone again by the midsummer gathering, and has asked Dame Cecily Ambler for it; she has refused.

Dame Cecily Ambler wants the First-Stone leaf gone from her house: the True Line's pilgrims have begun to stand at her door to look at it, and she is afraid of them. She will not be seen giving it to the True Line, because her son Godric and the Seated Houses would never forgive it, and because her husband asked her on his deathbed to keep it.

When Tuhuḍo of the Ninth-Ring House refused the True Line's petition to read the oldest house rolls, Godric Ambler read the refusal aloud from the archive stair to the True Line's petitioners, Ruʻo among them, and laughed.

At the new-moon gathering at the Founding Stone, before the pilgrims, Godric Ambler answered Ruʻo's charge that his father had bought a stolen leaf by saying that the True Line's pure blood was bought, like everything else at Firststone. Ruʻo has told the pilgrims that Godric spat on the Stone.
facts.when: after c-c-l1b-n8 (the pair's first card; 12 days before F1 is offered)

facts.text: Among the pilgrims of the pure blood, Ruʻo's word at the Founding Stone is taken as the True Line's own.
The young pilgrims have sworn to take a lock of Godric Ambler's hair at the Founding Stone, by force if he will not kneel and give it, the next time he rides the Firststone road.

Godric Ambler never touched or spat on the Founding Stone. Ruʻo says he did so the pilgrims will take Godric's words as a desecration and not as an answer; the pilgrims who stood nearest saw that he did not.
Last autumn the green took Rushmere, an edge hamlet below the Green Wall; its people were turned away from every gate in the Vale.

The band in the Mount's west quarry are Rushmere folk under Rufus Croome, driven out of their old ground when the green took their hamlet; they take what they need from whoever has no one to answer for them.
This spring the lower holdings under the Mount stopped paying the Mount's tithe, and the Mount's armed brothers stopped riding their lanes.
Rufus Croome's band has burned two hayricks in the lower holdings and taken their seed corn; Hodge Marley's is the last holding with any left.
Brookend paid Rufus Croome's band in grain to move on from its folds, and Bartle Ruck told them the lower holdings had stopped paying the Mount and had no one to ride for them.
Isolde of the Old Gate House has set woodmen to fell the hanging wood on the estate of the half-empty house below the Mount and sell the oak; the wood holds the slope above Coldharbour Lane.

The project is flawed: the hanging wood's oaks are old and many are heart-rotten, so felled and hauled down the Mount they will fetch less than the felling costs, and with the roots dead the slope will come down onto Coldharbour Lane in the first wet winter.
Hotorìṭo the High Priest will forbid any felling on the Mount's hill, on which he reckons the hanging wood stands, if Coldharbour Lane sends two of its young men to the Armed Nave's racks.

The Pilgrims' Stair is worn out and neglected: frost has been lifting its treads for three winters, the drains under them are choked, and no one has relaid a tread since the Mount stopped paying its stair-mason.
Two summers ago the stair-porters gave a month's wages to a mason from Oathford who relaid the bottom flight of the Pilgrims' Stair with rubble and left.
The middle flight of the Pilgrims' Stair has slid; porters and pilgrims now climb the Mount by the long cart road.
This spring the Fenby house began cutting a drain from Sedgemere to the river, to empty the mere and put its bed to meadow.

The project is flawed: Sedgemere's bed is deep peat, and drained it will shrink below the river and flood back every winter, so the meadow will never pay for the drain; but the summer it is dry, the stilt lane's wells and eel-traps go with it.
Davin Coe, a Horaro boat-builder of the stilt lane, has told the lane he is taking his family to the reef coast before winter.

Davin Coe sold the stilt lane's old landing-right on Sedgemere's bank to the Fenby house last winter, for coin enough to take his family to the reef coast; the drain could not have been cut across the landing without it. The lane does not know.
Roderick Hartwell, head of the Hartwell house at Ashring, died at the end of winter.
Forty years ago the Hartwell house's stone grew through the walls of the Corder house beside it; the Corders became lodgers in their own rooms, and Annis Corder later married Roderick Hartwell.
Tristram Hartwell claims the whole Hartwell house as his father's heir; Annis Corder claims the east wing, the swallowed Corder rooms, as her widow's portion and her own house's by right.

Both are partly right. The swallowed rooms of the east wing were the Corder house's by its own line in the archive, which has never been struck; the Hartwell stone that grew round them was tended by Hartwells for forty years.
The Vale wayside shrine is kept: its keeper, Eldreth Fowle, lives in the hut behind it.
The Mount keeps a checkpoint of lay brothers at the Vale wayside shrine, questioning pilgrims on the road about heresy; those carrying the Low Shrine's tokens are turned back.
Since spring the Vale wayside shrine's offering box has been found light at every month's emptying, though the pilgrims say they gave.
The checkpoint's sergeant blames Perkin Fowle, who sleeps in the shrine porch, and has said he will take him to the Mount for the theft.
The offering box's hasp is opened with the Mount's key, which the checkpoint's lay brothers keep for the monthly emptying; the hasp has never been forced.

Jarvis Mold, the youngest of the checkpoint's lay brothers, opens the box with the Mount's key after the keeper sleeps and takes the coin. The Mount has paid the checkpoint's brothers in nothing but bread since spring, and he sends the coin to his mother, whose holding owes the tithe-house.
The Tide Houses at Reefhold have barred Last Wave Qotiro from their quays and channel: any boat that carries one, and any pilot who brings one through, loses its berth at Reefhold.
Zillah Dunford, an envoy of Textrim's Height, waits at the landing stair under the Lantern Rock to be brought to the Raft of Captains to bargain for grain.
The fleet's grain hulks put out from the Anchorage for Openharbour at the month's end.
Zillah Dunford is what Demelza Pascoe says: the Height's envoy, come to buy grain for the winter, with nothing else in her charge.
The captains of the Raft mean to refuse Zillah Dunford: Juliana Whitlock has told them the fleet cannot be seen dealing with the Last Wave while it needs Reefhold's quays.
The Penhallow council house has begun cutting a new graving dock into its own yard ground, against the fish-lanes, to take the biggest hulls in the harbour.
Constance Penhallow has offered every fish-lanes household a purse to be gone before the spring tides.
The Penhallow dock is flawed: its cut runs below the fish-lanes' footings in soft harbour silt, and at the spring tides the sea will come up through the lanes' cellars and slump the dock's own walls.
Nan Gully means to take the Penhallow purse for her eel-smoke house and go; Dobbin Rusk and Mabon Quayle mean to stay and fight the dock.
The Openharbour reading room keeps the Unchained Quay roll: the name and year of every freed bondsman who has added a link to the Quay's railings.
The twelfth page of the Unchained Quay roll is in a newer hand than the pages around it, and Elowen Embry did not order it copied.

Raymond Thew, a buyer's agent from the Chainmarket, has come to Openharbour with a bond paper for a Qotiro runaway he says is the shipwright Gabriel Sowerby, and has asked to read the Unchained Quay roll for the year Gabriel says he added his link.

Lucius Vell re-wrote the twelfth page of the Unchained Quay roll to hide an older false line: twenty-two years ago Hepzibah Lunn, then the roll's clerk, entered Gabriel Sowerby, a runaway from the Chainmarket, as a freedman who had added his link, though he never stood before the council. Lucius did it so the page would pass Raymond Thew's reading and Gabriel would not be given up.
On the night before its launching, the cradle under Ceinwen Tregear's new pilot-cutter was knocked out, and the hull slid and stove its planks on the slip.
The Long Strand says Rufus Penwarden did it, and the pilots' hall has stopped Ceinwen Tregear's payments until it's settled.
The yard's night-watch walked Rufus Penwarden off the Long Strand at the second bell, before the cradle fell.

Ewan Larch, a sawyer at the Penhallow yard, knocked out the cradle: he meant to wreck the Penhallow galley on the next slip before the house's surveyor found the green timber he had put in its frames for Gilbert Mardle's coin, and in the dark he knocked the wrong cradle.
Seven years ago Amos Wetherell took the Vale house's Market Road warehouse on a written lease from its factor, Lark Gosling: rent each quarter-day, and the roof kept sound by the house.
Lark Gosling says Amos Wetherell has broken the lease by paying two seasons short, and means to put him out at the next quarter-day and let the warehouse to a bidder at twice the rent.

Both are partly right: Amos did pay two seasons short, which the lease lets the house end it for; but Lark Gosling took the Vale house's roof money for those two seasons and never sent the thatchers, and the rain spoiled the stock Amos would have paid it with.
Dilys Pratt's carter family sleep in the warehouse loft on Amos Wetherell's word, and go out with him if he goes.

Before Odette Calloway at the tavern-yard ring, Tegwen Hanna and Mostyn Carrow swore that a wagon race on the coast road, a loaded salt-wain each to the first mile-cairn and back, decides which of their crews holds the salt-house hauling right this season.
Eleven seasons ago Tegwen Hanna's crew took the salt-house hauling from Mostyn Carrow's father's crew by hauling at a third less, and the old Carrow crew broke up.
Mostyn Carrow has steady hauling elsewhere and doesn't need the salt-house right; he swore to the race to take it from Tegwen Hanna for what her crew did to his father's.

Tegwen Hanna has promised Aled Gower that if he wins the race she'll tear up his note for the team he drives; she can't, because she has already sold the note to Euphemia Grose to pay her crew's wages.
Ianto Brine keeps the Notch market for the Night Market.
Word has gone round Smugglers' Notch that someone sold the place of the next market.
Bridget Lowe, captain of the Saltmarket council's quay-watch, has sworn in extra watchmen to raid the night market at Smugglers' Notch, and the market's people have heard it comes tonight.
Nobody sold the market: Bridget Lowe found it herself, by counting the carts that cross the Saltmarket weighbridge after dark and following one down the cliff path.
Demelza Rosewarne, the finest deep diver on the Reefhold reef, died in her stilt house.
Cadan Rosewarne has said he will burn his mother's dive-book on her sending-raft at the next new moon, so that her deep beds rest with her.
Demelza Rosewarne's dive-book is the only record of where her deep kelp beds lie and at which tides she dived them.
By the reef's custom a diver's book is her heir's to keep or burn, and Demelza asked Cadan, before witnesses, to burn hers.
The dive-book has already been copied: Kerensa Rosewarne copied it page by page the winter before she sailed with the Far Sails, and keeps the copy aboard her boat.

Kerensa Rosewarne has come ashore from the fleet and claimed her mother's deep beds before the season's speaker, saying she can dive them by her mother's own book; Cadan says the beds rest with their mother.
Kerensa Rosewarne sailed with the Far Sails the spring their mother first fell sick, and left Cadan to nurse her alone.

Both are partly right: Demelza did ask Cadan to let her beds rest, but for one year only, for the deep kelp to grow back; the last page of her book leaves the beds 'to whichever of my two dives them as I did'.
Since the Speaker's Deck he built sank two hands in its third year instead of one, Reefhold has said that Caradoc Polwhele built it hollow and pocketed the piling coin.
The next Speaker's Deck must be built this generation, and the speaker gives the work to a deck-wright whose name Reefhold trusts.

The stain is exaggerated: the deck sank fast because the lagoon floor under its east pilings is soft, which Caradoc found and reported, and he pocketed nothing. But the name Reefhold is weighing hides something real: for forty years Caradoc's pilings were set by Qotiro bondsmen the Boscawen house lent him, and three of them drowned setting the last deck's east pilings. No one has ever said their names.
Peran Trevail knows what lies under the east pilings, and will not say it in public.
Kasimir Dree, a Qotiro bondsman of the Boscawen house, has run, and the house's steward Hartley Pengelly is searching the stilts for him.
Kasimir Dree saw Hartley Pengelly hold a runaway bondsman under in the Boscawen lagoon until he drowned.
Kasimir is what Petra Marlowe says he is: a bondsman running for his life because of what he saw, with nothing else on him and no one sent after him but the steward.
The Boscawen house keeps a great deepcoil in its walled lagoon, fed for three generations as the house's pride; it is the house's, and killing it is a crime.
For a month something has broken the outer weirs at night, eaten their catch and drowned a net-boy, and the weir crews have seen a deepcoil's back in the channel by the Boscawen lagoon.
The Boscawen lagoon's sea-gate opens on the channel beside the outer weirs.
Tomas Keast has been prising the Boscawen lagoon's sea-gate bars at night to slip in and take the house's ribbonbacks; the bars he loosened are how the deepcoil gets out.
Since the thaw, the Wardens who drink from the Wellstone well have come down with a griping sickness, and two of the salvage crew can no longer work.
Bedwyr Ashlin wants the well filled and the salvage camp moved down to the Wall; Ithel Morgan, Wellstone-born, will not leave its well, and Hoqa sides with him: the line needs a camp past the Wall.
The Wellstone well went bad when Teilo Brannan dug his charcoal pits on the slope above its spring this spring; the lye from the pits' wet ash seeps into the spring.
Gorran Ketch's scavengers were driven out of their old ground when the green took their village, Ditchend, two winters ago, and have lived since on what they strip from the lost villages.
Since the thaw, scavengers out of the drowned orchard have come to the Soft Hollow by night, stripped the keepsakes the grieving hang in the Listening Trees, and taken the Hollow's stores.

Last autumn the Green Wall's Wardens caught Gorran Ketch's band stripping the salvage grounds the Wall lives on and, on Haʻo's word, drove them past Wellstone into the green rather than take them in at the Wall; the band has lived off the Soft Hollow since.
Cai Ashlin has sworn to the green.
Tirion Ashlin is sworn to the green and listens in the trees.
Gwilym Ashlin, a Warden, was lost to the green on the edge path beyond Wellstone; his name is on the Names Post.
Since their father was lost, Bedwyr Ashlin of the Green Wall has not spoken to his brother Cai, who went to the Soft Hollow to hear him in the trees.
facts.when: since two years before the story

facts.text: The Mount's inquisitors have named the Soft Hollow's Listening Trees for burning before the season turns.

Bedwyr never forgave Cai for marrying Tirion, a listener of the Soft Hollow, and when their father was lost and Cai went to hear him in the trees, Bedwyr stopped speaking to him. He keeps away for a reason he has never said: Cai has sworn to the green, and as long as the brothers don't speak, the Wardens never ask Bedwyr where his brother stands.
Garmon Dyer has sworn to the green, and listens in the trees beside the tower he built.
Watchtower Ash has been taken by the green: its signal fire hasn't been lit since the thaw, and the line of towers has a gap between the Green Wall and the Hush grove.
The newest of the Year Cairns stands farther in from the old line than any year's before it: the green is coming faster.

Watchtower Ash went quiet because its footing ring was carted off: the winter it stood empty, Pasco Hendry carted the outer footing stones to his edge farm for a byre wall, and the green's roots came in under the bare footing and split the tower's base.
Garmon Dyer is the only one living who knows how Watchtower Ash's footing was laid, and he will not set a stone.

Totkit Sea-crosser's war-dogs, bred at the Proving Ground for the war its young warriors want, are kept in the kennels on the Rim above the Height's goat terraces; this autumn they have been running down to the terraces at night and killing goats.
The Proving Ground's war-dog kennels sit on the Rim directly above the Height's goat terraces: the preserve is next door.
A stretch of the kennel wall above the terraces has fallen, and Selwyn Hendra has said nothing of it to the war-chief.
Daveth Pascoe stoned one of the war-dogs to death on the terraces twenty days before the story, and the Proving Ground's young warriors want him brought to the Circle for it.
Textrim, High Priestess, will make Totkit Sea-crosser pen his dogs only if Loveday Pascoe gives her son Daveth up to the Proving Ground's Circle to answer for the dog he killed.

The Step spring went bad when the Brine Step moved Kerensa Treloar's brine-pans uphill of it this autumn: brine and lye from the pans now seep through the rock into the water the Ash Step drinks and quenches its blades in.
Talan Opie had the brine-pans moved off the Brine Step's own cistern after it soured last spring, and told the Ash Step nothing.

Textrim, High Priestess, holds Austol Spargo and his lad Kenan Rowse in the cells under the ziggurat, on Tavin Crake's word that he saw him on the trail-gate steps counting the Height's spears for the crown's recruiter.

Austol Spargo was counting salt-sacks, not spears: he was tallying the forge salt the gate-watch would sell him against the sacks his mules could carry down, and Tavin Crake, who cannot read a tally-stick and sees a lowland spy in every lowlander, took his notches for a count of the war-band.

Mawgan Rosewarne has challenged Peran Bolitho in the Height's duel circle on blood terms, saying Peran turned his lowland-born mother away from the trail gate and shamed her before the watch; Ithel Nancarrow has set the bout for the next fire-night.
The slight is a cover: the war-band has promised Mawgan Rosewarne the trail gate if Peran Bolitho falls, and means to shut it to every lowland trader before the winter, so that hunger forces the war.
Gawen Thrale's band took Kerra Hosking on the lowland trail below the Height and holds her at the burned smoke hall, to make her father Selevan Hosking forge them a load of the Height's blades.
The band took Kerra Hosking as leverage over her father: they want forty blades from Selevan Hosking's forge.
It is as it looks: Gawen Thrale's band wants the blades and nothing else, to arm themselves for catching on the Rim now the Chainmarket will not stand behind them.
Last winter Sabra Venning turned Locryn Penhallow's son out of the Ash Gully camp for breaking the hunt's peace; he went down to the lowlands and has not come back.

Before Imogen Morrow in the step-hall, Sabra Venning, for the Ash Gully camp's families, and Locryn Penhallow swore that a bout to yield decides which household holds the first shield of Ironstep's winter guard-company.
The first shield of Ironstep's winter guard-company leads the company the lowland caravan-masters hire, and draws a double share of the hire: a hungry winter's bread.
Locryn Penhallow doesn't need the double share: he fights to keep the first shield from Sabra Venning, because she turned his son out of the Ash Gully camp and his son has not come home.

Mirabel Coldwell sells Ansel Whitby, Gisela Lorne's steward, first refusal on every bond made at Breakwall; Ansel now says Piran Calder was already on Gisela's tally when Mirabel took his bond, so her paper broke their agreement.
Gisela Lorne has told Ansel Whitby she will call his own note and put him in her teams if he does not bring her more hands for the iron haul by the next breach sitting.

Ansel Whitby's claim is the false one: the mark beside Piran Calder's name on Gisela Lorne's tally was made by Ansel's own tally-man after Piran sold his bond to Mirabel; Mirabel's paper is good, and she means to sell Piran on to the Block at twice his price.
Hicca Mallet, the Block's weigher's apprentice, was found dead at the foot of the Block on a sale-morning, its top step loose under him.

Steren Chegwin loosened the Block's top step the night before the sale, to kill Treve Polwhele, who climbs it first every sale-morning and had found that Steren writes children down as grown on the bills of sale; that morning Hicca Mallet went up first to chalk the weights.
The drovers' quarter blames Elestren Pellam, who quarrelled with Hicca Mallet over a ribbon the night before he died, and means to turn her out at the next sale.
Arthek Carne, then a bonded pit-fighter, killed Jacca Trethewey in a blood bout in the old pit below the Block, matched for a lord's buyer, nine winters before the story.
Arthek Carne holds the third rung of the Chainmarket circuit ladder.
Before Edmund Gilchrist, Arthek Carne and Colan Trethewey swore under Society rules to a bout to yield for Arthek's rung, which Colan has asked to fight in the old pit below the Block.
Colan Trethewey doesn't want the rung: he wants to see Arthek Carne break, to watch the man who killed his brother stand in the same pit and be afraid.
Three bonded people drowned crossing the Bogford ford with a Chainmarket coffle in a spring flood, nine winters before the story.
The drovers' quarter says Tristan Rodda let a coffle drown at the Bogford ford, and no lord's buyer will give him a drove now.

The stain is false: the coffle that drowned at the Bogford ford was on another drover's watch, Tristan Rodda's late partner; the tavern-talk muddled the two names when the partner died, and nobody set it straight.
Nine captives, Nessa Grigg among them, slipped their chains at the Sedge pens on a moonless night and are gone into the sedge.

Jenkin Curnow, the pens' night-hand, opened the chains: Nessa Grigg is his sister, brought in on the last raid, and he could not stand to see her marked for the lord's buyer; he freed them all so no one would ask which one he meant.
The Gap clan and the ore-clan have been at odds since ore was found at the edge of the Gap pasture last autumn.

Both claims hold in part: the Gap clan has summered its herds on the pasture since the old cairns were set, and the ore-clan's right to cut under it is older still; the ore at its edge was found by a lowland prospector, Joss Rendle, whom Madron Keast had sat at the Gap hut's fire and shown the high ground, to have lowland coin behind his clan against the ore-clan's right.

Each spring the High Snows run the guides' race up the cliff stair and over the Gap and back; Cardew Mably gives the year's guide's mark, the right to take lowlanders over the passes for pay, to the first runner home who carries a clan's token.
Lanyon Hext runs for the same thing Cubert Penna does, the mark and the living it brings, and he needs it more: his lame mother and two small sisters eat by what he carries over the passes.
Brannoc Clemmow wants out of the guides' race: his knee went on the ice last winter and he knows he can't make the Gap.

Joss Rendle sat at the Gap pass hut's fire as Udy Keast's guest, then led a Great House surveyor up the Gap by the guides' marks, and struck Udy down when he barred the hut's door to them; Udy left the hut, and it has stood cold since.
Arscott Mewton, elder of the Foothill post, will not let the clans' complaint against Joss Rendle be heard at the post; he takes Joss's coin.
Joss Rendle now buys the clans' ore at the Foothill post, the one place the High Snows sell to lowlanders.

Udy Keast had a hand in it: at his brother Madron's bidding he had shown Joss Rendle the Gap's guides' marks himself, so the lowlander could find the ore and bring coin behind the Gap clan; the marks Joss led the surveyor by were the ones Udy taught him at the hut's fire.
Jonah Tresize swore before the crews in the Long Shed that if Harvey Anstey's crew stands against the strike, he will burn their half of the yard with their hired teams in it.

Both are partly right about what started it: Harvey Anstey hired Silas Pennock's teams on Counting-House notes because his own crew's teams were sold to pay its winter debts, not to sell the strike; and Jonah Tresize is right that the notes bind Harvey's crew to vote against it.
Gethin Rowe lost his brother in the last crews' feud at Carter's Rest, when two crews fought over the Long Shed's upper stalls, thirty winters before the story.

fault_line.virtue violated: the Open Hand genuinely frees people, and the Scales Hall's pride is honest weight; Feyesh's notes stand on people weighed as stock in the cellar's second books

faces.plain: After Morwen Carter died, her widower Aldous Brede claimed her change-yard at Carter's Rest against her son Doruḍoqu, on a later will he says she made before the Counting-House's factor, Silas Pennock. The yard is shut until the claim is weighed.

Silas Pennock, the Counting-House's factor, has bought up the Road Crews' team-notes and called them due before the Long Shed vote. Crews that stood for the strike and can't pay are losing their teams and wagons under the notes, from Wainyard to the Saltmarket quay.
faces.despite_you: Though the Long Shed's teams were saved from the bad water, Silas Pennock had already bought the notes on them; he called them due before the vote, and the crews that stood for the strike lost their teams and wagons under the notes all the same, from Wainyard to the Saltmarket quay.

faces.plain: Under hauling contracts the Counting-House bought from the Free Lords, the gate-men at Breakwall and the Chainmarket have turned the Road Crews off the Marches roads. The Free Lords' bog iron and timber now go out with teamsters hired at the Chainmarket, under Nerys Saltonstall's seal.

Feyesh has bought up the notes of the striking crew-bosses' families, and on his coin Doruḍoqu's kin have disowned him before the whole island. His sister Ilsa Carter's sworn letter, naming him the Counting-House's man who sold the strike, has gone out from the Wayhouse at Highcrossing to every Lending Wall, beside letters like it naming other striking crew-bosses; and his uncle Teague Carter has asked the Ninth Ring to strike him from the Carter line.

With councillors' votes bought on Counting-House notes, the Open Council at Openharbour has outlawed the Road Crews' strike, barred every crew that struck from the Open Hand's yards, struck Doruḍoqu from the foremanship and seated Silas Pennock as foreman in his place. The council's harbour guard has taken the five crew-bosses who would not stand down into the harbour cells, the crews' common chest has been lodged at the Counting-House, and Feyesh has asked the council to lodge its own treasury there at its next sitting.
faces.target: Ilsa Carter's letter (c-c-main-4a-3) and the Carter house (c-c-main-4b-3)
faces.despite_you: Though Ilsa Carter had taken back her letter and the Carter line still stood in the rolls, the councillors Feyesh had paid voted as they were paid: the strike is outlawed, the striking crews are barred from the Open Hand's yards, Doruḍoqu is struck from the foremanship with Silas Pennock seated in his place, the five crew-bosses are in the harbour cells, the crews' chest is at the Counting-House, and Feyesh has asked for the council's treasury.

return_variants.won (justice done, ruined, amends, drive: Feyesh has answered for the bought votes, but the council's ruling stands until it sits again: Silas Pennock keeps the Long Shed's keys, the crews are split, and Doruḍoqu's son drives for the man who replaced him.
return_variants.forgave (talked down, or forgives): Doruḍoqu let the reckoning go to keep the crews' chest whole; Feyesh's council stands, Silas Pennock keeps the Long Shed, and Kit Carter drives for him.
return_variants.lost (sides with the wrongdoer, or fails: Feyesh's council stands: the strike is outlawed, Silas Pennock is foreman, the crews' chest is in the Counting-House, and Kit Carter drives for the man who replaced his father.
